timelineEvents.title: Private study and first Berlin networks
timelineEvents.label: 1926–1930 · Berlin study and networks
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper builds his Berlin career through private study with Moriz Mayer-Mahr and Walther Gmeindl, early publications, and collaboration with Fritz Rotter.
timelineEvents.longDescription: After moving to Berlin, Kaper developed his professional position through private study with pianist Moriz Mayer-Mahr and composer-conductor Walther Gmeindl, while also entering the German-language song market through Fritz Rotter and early publications under the title “Dr. Kaper.”

timelineEvents.title: Marriage
timelineEvents.label: 30 June 1927 · Marriage in Berlin
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper marries Eleonora Sirot in Berlin.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Kaper marries Eleonora de domo Sirot in Berlin on June 30.

timelineEvents.title: Róża Etkin performs Kaper’s Sonatina in Berlin
timelineEvents.label: 1927 · Etkin performs Sonatina
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Róża Etkin performs Kaper’s Sonatina in Berlin, a performance later confirmed by Kaper’s oral-history recollection.
timelineEvents.longDescription: A 1927 German press notice documents the Berlin performance context, and Kaper’s later oral-history recollection identifies the work as his Sonatina.

timelineEvents.title: Jazz Piano Partnership
timelineEvents.label: 1928 · Jazz piano partnership
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper records jazz-influenced piano duo arrangements with Hermann Bick for Polydor.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Along with Hermann Bick (Bieck), he records piano duo arrangements for Deutsche Grammophon/Polydor. These sessions showcase contemporary American jazz standards including "Miss Annabelle Lee," "The Varsity Drag," and "The Song Is Ended." The collaboration blends classical virtuosity with jazz spontaneity, creating sophisticated interpretations that avoid the trivial "novelty piano" style of the era.

timelineEvents.title: First publications and recordings with Fritz Rotter
timelineEvents.label: 1929 · Rotter publications and recordings
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper’s tangos and foxtrots with Fritz Rotter appear in German and Viennese editions.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Tangos and foxtrots by "Dr. Kaper" published in German and Viennese editions.

timelineEvents.title: Involvement in Polish cultural life in Berlin
timelineEvents.label: 1929 · Polish cultural life in Berlin
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper remains active in Berlin’s Polish cultural life, including work with the Harmonia choir.
timelineEvents.longDescription: "Kurier Warszawski" reports on a concert by the Berlin choir "Harmonia", directed by Kaper.

timelineEvents.title: ERKLA-Quartett concert review in Hamborn
timelineEvents.label: 10 Dec 1929 · ERKLA in Hamborn
timelineEvents.shortDescription: A Rhein- und Ruhrzeitung review documents Kaper’s appearance with the ERKLA four-piano ensemble in Hamborn, alongside Giuliano Pomeranz, then performing as Julian Pomeranc, Aleksander Zakin, and Leopold Mittmann.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Dr. Funk’s review “Jazz auf vier Flügeln” in the Rhein- und Ruhrzeitung, 10 December 1929, p. 12, documents an ERKLA concert in Hamborn. It names Kaper alongside Giuliano Pomeranz, then performing as Julian Pomeranc, Aleksander Zakin, and Leopold Mittmann.

timelineEvents.title: Bick & Kaper at Berlin premiere
timelineEvents.label: 1929 · Bick & Kaper at Berlin premiere
timelineEvents.shortDescription: The Bick und Kaper piano duo plays at a Berlin film premiere and attracts press attention.
timelineEvents.longDescription: The jazz piano duo Bick und Kaper performs at the Ufa-Theater "Universum" in Berlin, opening the premiere of "Der Adjutant des Zaren." The Rhein- und Ruhrzeitung writes: "Their technique is astonishing."

timelineEvents.title: First compositions for film
timelineEvents.label: 1930 · First film compositions
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper begins composing for cinema with music for early German sound films.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Music for "Alraune", directed by Richard Oswald and "Der Korvettenkapitän" directed by Rudolf Walther-Fein

timelineEvents.title: Meeting Walter Jurmann
timelineEvents.label: 1931 · Meeting Walter Jurmann
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper meets Walter Jurmann, launching the songwriting partnership that defines his European film career.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Introduced by Fritz Rotter, marking the start of the Jurmann–Kaper duo. First joint project: “Die große Attraktion,” directed by Max Reichmann. Kaper composes the hit slow fox “Du warst mir ein Roman” for Richard Tauber.

timelineEvents.title: Flourishing Berlin collaboration
timelineEvents.label: 1932 · Berlin collaboration flourishes
timelineEvents.shortDescription: The Jurmann–Kaper partnership flourishes across German films and popular songs.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Numerous German films with Jurmann–Kaper music, including "Hochzeitsreise zu dritt", "Skandal in der Parkstraße", "Es wird schon wieder besser", "Der glückliche Herr Fünf".

timelineEvents.title: Migration from Berlin via Vienna to Paris
timelineEvents.label: 1933 · Berlin–Vienna–Paris migration
timelineEvents.shortDescription: After Nazi persecution intensifies, Kaper and Jurmann leave Berlin and relocate toward Paris.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Following Nazi persecution, Kaper and Jurmann flee Berlin after UFA terminates Jewish employees' contracts. Decisive moment: Kaper and his wife are attacked by Nazi gang on main Berlin street. Both composers relocate to Paris.

timelineEvents.title: Paris period
timelineEvents.label: 1933–1934 · Paris period
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper works in Paris for French producers, contributing songs and film music with Jurmann.
timelineEvents.longDescription: About 18 months of work for French producers; film "Les Nuits moscovites" with hits like "Natascha" and "On n'aime qu'une fois"; compositions for revue Parade de France.

timelineEvents.title: At the Salabert studio in Montrouge
timelineEvents.label: 23 Dec 1933 · Salabert studio, Montrouge
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper and Jurmann are reported at the Salabert studio in Montrouge during a Paris recording session.
timelineEvents.longDescription: "Paris-Soir" reports on Kaper and Jurmann present at the Salabert recording studio in Montrouge, where Henri Garat records songs for his latest film.

timelineEvents.title: Cocktail with Jan Kiepura
timelineEvents.label: 17 Feb 1934 · Cocktail with Jan Kiepura
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper and Jurmann attend a Paris reception for Jan Kiepura as composers of Tout pour l’amour.
timelineEvents.longDescription: In February, Kaper attends a cocktail reception for Jan Kiepura at the George V in Paris together with Walter Jurmann. A contemporary press report names them among the invited guests and identifies them as the composers of the music for Tout pour l’amour.

timelineEvents.title: European afterlife
timelineEvents.label: 1934–1936 · European afterlife
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Jurmann–Kaper films and songs continue circulating in Europe after the composers leave for America.
timelineEvents.longDescription: While the composers head to America, their European films and songs continue to circulate. In September 1934, "Madame wird kinderlieb" still plays in Stuttgart with Jurmann and Kaper credited — despite Nazi purges. In France, "Tout pour l'amour" with Kiepura screens as late as 1936; the Journal de Vichy calls their music "infiniment plaisante."

timelineEvents.title: Earliest documented collaboration with Fritz Rotter
timelineEvents.label: First Rotter trace
timelineEvents.shortDescription: A 1926 manuscript of Hätt’ ich einen Kammerdiener documents an early collaboration between Kaper and Fritz Rotter, before sound film became his main professional platform.
timelineEvents.longDescription: The manuscript credit for Hätt’ ich einen Kammerdiener places Kaper beside Fritz Rotter at an early point in his Berlin years. It is an important transitional event: Rotter linked Kaper to the practical economy of the German hit song—publishers, performers, promotion, and sheet-music circulation—before those skills were absorbed into the machinery of early sound film. It also explains why Rotter later became the mediator who brought Kaper and Walter Jurmann together.

timelineEvents.title: Alraune as Kaper’s first documented sound-film commission
timelineEvents.label: Alraune and sound film
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Alraune marks Kaper’s first clearly documented entry into early sound film, through songs rather than background scoring in the later Hollywood sense.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Kaper’s first documented sound-film work belongs to the early phase of cinema in which the film composer’s task was still closely tied to song production. Alraune, Richard Oswald’s 1930 sound remake, did not yet require the later Hollywood model of continuous underscoring. Instead, Kaper contributed songs that could serve the film while also entering the wider economy of printed scores, records, performers, and radio.

timelineEvents.title: The Sängerfilm and the star-singer circuit
timelineEvents.label: Sängerfilm circuit
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper and Jurmann’s songs entered the Sängerfilm economy, where screen performance, star singers, sheet music, records, radio, and dance-band repertory reinforced one another.
timelineEvents.longDescription: The Kaper–Jurmann partnership developed inside the commercial ecology of early European musical film. Their songs for productions associated with singers such as Richard Tauber and Jan Kiepura were not simply film numbers: they were designed to travel beyond the screen as printed music, recordings, radio items, and repertory for performers. This star-singer circuit explains why the duo’s European experience later appeared useful to MGM, which read it through the promotional language of Viennese musical competence.

timelineEvents.title: Multiple-language versions and transnational sound-film production
timelineEvents.label: Transnational sound film
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Before 1933, Kaper and Jurmann were already working within the multiple-language version system that linked Babelsberg, Joinville, Vienna, and other European production centres.
timelineEvents.longDescription: The practice of producing parallel language versions was one of the key industrial conditions of early sound cinema. It allowed music to move more easily than dialogue across national markets, even when lyrics, singers, and performance contexts changed. Kaper and Jurmann’s work in this system gave their songs and professional skills a transnational character before their forced departure from Germany.
